title: How do you train contractors and temporary workers?
description: How to train contractors and temporary workers: split duties between agency and host in writing, train before work starts, verify competence, share records.
shortAnswer: Train contractors and temporary workers by agreeing in writing which party delivers which training before anyone starts, with the supplying employer usually covering general safety and job skills and the host covering site specific hazards, procedures and emergency arrangements. Verify that both parts happened and that the worker can do the task, deliver it in a language they understand, share records between the parties, and treat these workers like your own staff for training purposes.
keyTakeaways: Responsibility is shared, not transferred. The US Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) treats staffing agencies and host employers as jointly responsible for temporary workers' training.
The usual split: the agency or contractor provides general safety and trade training; the host provides site specific training, because it controls the hazards.
Train before work begins. OSHA, the EU temporary workers directive and Australian work health and safety laws all expect information and training before the worker is exposed.
Put the split in the contract, and require each party to tell the other when its training is complete.
Verify, do not assume. A card or certificate from another employer shows past training, not knowledge of your site.

sections.heading: Who is responsible for training contractors and temporary workers?

blocks.text: Both the supplying employer and the host business are responsible, each for the hazards and tasks it can control. The legal frameworks in the main markets reach the same answer from different directions.

items: **United States.** OSHA states that the staffing agency and the host employer are joint employers of temporary workers and are "jointly responsible for maintaining a safe work environment," including ensuring that OSHA's training, hazard communication and recordkeeping requirements are met. It adds that host employers "must treat temporary workers like any other workers in terms of training and safety and health protections" ([OSHA, Protecting Temporary Workers](https://www.osha.gov/temporaryworkers)).

**European Union.** Directive 91/383/EEC aims to give fixed term and temporary agency workers the same level of safety and health protection as other workers in the user undertaking. Before such a worker starts, the user undertaking must inform them of the risks (Article 3), and each worker must receive sufficient training appropriate to the job, taking account of their qualifications and experience (Article 4). The user must tell the agency the qualifications required and the specific features of the job (Article 7) ([Directive 91/383/EEC](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:31991L0383)). The OSH Framework Directive separately requires employers to ensure that workers from outside undertakings working in their establishment have in fact received appropriate instructions ([Article 12(2)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:31989L0391); see [EU OSH Framework Directive training](/regulations/eu-osh-framework-directive-training)).

**Australia.** Under the model Work Health and Safety (WHS) Act, more than one person can hold the same duty, each must discharge it to the extent they can influence and control the matter (section 16), and each must consult, cooperate and coordinate with the others (section 46). Safe Work Australia's consultation code applies this directly to contractors and labor hire workers ([Safe Work Australia](https://www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/doc/model-code-practice-work-health-and-safety-consultation-cooperation-and-coordination); see [the WHS duty to provide training](/regulations/whs-act-duty-to-provide-training)).

blocks.text: Neither party can contract its way out. OSHA's Temporary Worker Initiative bulletin on training says the parties may divide responsibility, but "neither employer may avoid their ultimate responsibilities under the OSH Act by requiring another party to perform them" ([OSHA TWI Bulletin No. 4](https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/OSHA3859.pdf)).

sections.heading: How should training be split between the supplier and the host?

blocks.text: Split it by who controls the hazard and who is best placed to teach it. OSHA's bulletin describes the usual pattern: the staffing agency provides generic safety and health training, and the host provides site specific training because it controls the work methods, equipment and processes.

blocks.text: The supplier still has to check. OSHA says the staffing agency must have a reasonable basis for believing the host's training adequately addresses the hazards, and if it does not, should work with the host to provide adequate training, provide it itself, or remove its workers. Under OSHA's recordkeeping rule, the employer supervising day to day, usually the host, records the temporary worker's injuries.

sections.heading: What must happen before a contractor or temporary worker starts?

blocks.text: Information, site induction and task training must be complete before the worker is exposed to the hazard. OSHA's bulletin says training must be completed before the worker begins work on a project and must be in a language and vocabulary the worker understands. EU Directive 91/383/EEC requires risk information before the worker takes up any activity.

items: **Before placement:** the host specifies the tasks, hazards and required qualifications; the supplier confirms the worker has them and has had general training.
**On arrival:** the host checks identity and credentials, delivers the site induction (see [how to build a safety induction](/guides/how-to-build-a-safety-induction)), and confirms language needs.
**Before the task:** the host or competent supplier delivers task training and confirms competence by observation or questioning.
**During the assignment:** supervision proportionate to risk and inexperience; retraining before any new task or equipment.
**At the end:** records are exchanged and retained by both parties; access is removed.

blocks.title: Illustrative example drawn from OSHA's guidance
blocks.text: OSHA's training bulletin describes a fictional contractor that asked a staffing agency for unskilled laborers, then assigned three of them to remove roofing about 13 feet above the ground without fall protection or training. OSHA's analysis: the host had no reason to believe the workers were trained in fall protection and was best placed to provide jobsite specific training. The lesson is that the host's task assignment, not the agency's general training, determined what training was needed.

sections.heading: Does the same apply to non safety training?

blocks.text: Yes, the pattern repeats wherever a regime covers people who are not direct employees. Supplied workers who handle data, money, classified information or regulated products usually need the same role based training as employees doing the same work.

In US defense contracting, for example, the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM) makes a cleared temporary help supplier responsible for ensuring required initial and refresher briefings are provided to its cleared personnel, and allows either the supplier or the using contractor to conduct them ([32 CFR 117.12(j)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/32/117.12); see [NISPOM security training requirements](/regulations/nispom-security-training-requirements)). OSHA's recommended practices likewise say program awareness training should reach contractor, subcontractor and temporary agency workers as well as employees ([OSHA](https://www.osha.gov/safety-management/education-training)).

Practical test: if a supplied worker could cause the harm a training requirement exists to prevent, include them in the [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) for that role, and record who delivered each item.

sections.heading: What should the contract say about training?

blocks.text: The contract should make the split explicit and require evidence. OSHA recommends that staffing agencies and hosts set out their respective responsibilities for compliance with applicable standards in their contract, and that each party inform the other when training is completed. EU Directive 91/383/EEC allows the host's job details to appear in a contract of assignment.

items: The tasks, locations and equipment the worker may be assigned to, and a rule that new tasks require notice and retraining.
Required qualifications, licenses and prior training, with how they will be verified.
Which party delivers each training element, using a matrix like the one above.
Language and literacy arrangements, including interpreters.
Record content, format and exchange timing; retention responsibility for each party.
Incident and injury reporting routes, and a statement that neither party will discourage reporting.
The supplier's right to inspect the site and the host's training, and to withdraw workers.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry defines the knowledge a role requires independently of who employs the person in it, so a supplied worker can be assessed against the same concepts as an employee, with each item attributed to the party that delivered it. That makes split responsibility visible in one record. See [audit evidence](/platform/audit-evidence).

faqs.q: Can a host rely on a contractor's own training records?
faqs.a: Partly. Records can show that general and trade training happened, but they do not show knowledge of your site's hazards, procedures and emergency arrangements. Verify credentials, deliver site induction and task training, and confirm competence. OSHA expects each employer to address the hazards it is in a position to prevent and correct.

faqs.q: Do temporary workers need the same training as permanent staff?
faqs.a: For the same tasks and hazards, yes. OSHA says host employers must treat temporary workers like any other workers in terms of training. EU Directive 91/383/EEC aims for the same level of protection as other workers in the user undertaking, with training appropriate to the job and the worker's qualifications and experience.

The contract usually decides between businesses, but the worker should not bear the cost of required safety training. The EU OSH Framework Directive says required training may not be at workers' expense and must take place during working hours, and OSHA's publication on training requirements states that required training must be provided by and paid for by employers.

faqs.q: What if the agency thinks the host's training is inadequate?
faqs.a: OSHA's guidance says the agency should inform the host and work together to provide adequate training, provide the training itself, or remove its workers from the site. Having a representative on site does not transfer the host's responsibility for site specific training to the agency.

factCheck.claim: OSHA: staffing agency and host are joint employers; jointly responsible including training, hazard communication and recordkeeping; recommends contract terms setting out responsibilities; each employer considers hazards it can prevent and correct; agencies general training, hosts specific training; hosts must treat temporary workers like any other workers in terms of training.

TWI Bulletin No. 4: training completed before work begins and in a language and vocabulary the worker understands; parties may divide responsibility and should inform each other when complete; neither may avoid ultimate responsibilities; agency needs reasonable basis to believe host training adequate, else inform host, provide training, or remove workers; on-site agency representative does not transfer responsibility; host usually records injuries (1904.31(b)(2)); fictional roofing scenario about 13 feet.

Directive 91/383/EEC Article 2 same level of protection; Article 3 information before taking up activity; Article 4 sufficient training appropriate to the job taking account of qualifications and experience; Article 7 user specifies qualifications and job features to the temporary employment business, details may appear in a contract of assignment; Article 8 user responsible for conditions of work during assignment.
Directive 89/391/EEC Article 12(2): workers from outside undertakings must have in fact received appropriate instructions; Article 12(4): training not at workers' expense and during working hours.

Model WHS Act s16 more than one person can have a duty and each discharges it to extent of influence and control; s46 duty to consult, cooperate and coordinate with other duty holders; code section 4.4 on contractors and labour hire.
32 CFR 117.12(j): cleared temporary help supplier responsible for required briefings; supplier or using contractor may conduct them.
OSHA Recommended Practices action item 1: program awareness training for managers, supervisors, workers, and contractor, subcontractor and temporary agency workers.
OSHA 2254: all required training must be provided by and paid for by employers.
